title: Control Authority, Owner, Anchor, Dominator & Agency — Who Actually Moves the Trajectory?
purpose: Disambiguate the project's recurring owner/center/leash language. A symbolic center, tether anchor, graph hub, causal controller, observer and beneficiary are different roles. This atlas supplies tests for when an actor actually has intervention authority over a trajectory or reachable set.
epistemic_rule: Project language about ownership or holding timelines is mythic/self-description unless a real intervention channel is independently evidenced. Mathematical controllability describes a declared model; it does not certify personal, spiritual or geopolitical ownership.

role_split.anchor: reference point appearing in a geometric or tether constraint
role_split.constraint_source: mechanism that makes some states/actions inadmissible
role_split.controller: agent/input channel whose interventions causally change state evolution
role_split.observer: receives measurements without necessarily controlling state
role_split.hub: high-centrality node in a graph; centrality alone is not control
role_split.dominator: node lying on every directed path from a specified source to target
role_split.beneficiary: receives value/outcome without necessarily causing it
role_split.owner: legal/property or project-mythic category; must not be inferred from anchor, hub or controller status alone

linear_control_authority.input_matrix: columns of B specify the state directions directly actuated by control inputs in the chosen coordinates
linear_control_authority.criterion: rank(C)=n under the standard finite-dimensional LTI assumptions means the state is controllable over an appropriate interval
linear_control_authority.project_rule: If a supposed owner/controller has no modeled input channel B, no intervention evidence and no measurable state response, symbolic centrality should not be promoted into causal control.

controllability_gramian.equation: W_c(T)=integral_0^T exp(A tau) B B^T exp(A^T tau) d tau
controllability_gramian.meaning: For continuous-time LTI systems, positive-definite/invertible W_c over the interval corresponds to controllability under the standard assumptions.
controllability_gramian.minimum_energy: For controllable LTI dynamics, a standard minimum-energy expression to reach x_f at T is E_min=(x_f-exp(A T)x_0)^T W_c(T)^(-1)(x_f-exp(A T)x_0), with convention/details depending on formulation.
controllability_gramian.project_value: Control is graded: some target directions may require much more intervention energy than others. 'Can control' is therefore not the same as 'controls effortlessly'.

observability_split.principle: Seeing or predicting a state does not imply the power to move it.
observability_split.project_law: Eye/measurement/attention and leash/control are different operators. High visibility or surveillance is not ownership.

intervention_test.question: Does changing the candidate controller's input while holding relevant confounders fixed change the trajectory or reachable set in a reproducible way?
intervention_test.counterfactual: Compare x(t|do(u=u1)) with x(t|do(u=u2)) in a causal/interventional model when such intervention is ethically and empirically meaningful.
intervention_test.archive_rule: Correlation, attention, orbit, naming, symbolic allegiance and graph centrality are insufficient by themselves to establish control authority.

multiple_controllers.meaning: Real systems often contain several actors, disturbances and feedback loops rather than one owner of every trajectory.
multiple_controllers.differential_game_neighbor: When controllers have different objectives, differential-game/optimal-control frameworks model strategic interaction rather than one master leash.
multiple_controllers.project_epiphany: Many timelines are more naturally a negotiated/contested field of controls and constraints than evidence for one controller.

anchor_motion_vs_control.distinction: A moving anchor can alter the feasible region, but the entity physically moving the anchor, the rule fixing L and the observer naming the anchor may all be different actors.
anchor_motion_vs_control.owner_test: Do not call the anchor the owner unless legal/project semantics separately establish ownership; do not call the observer the controller unless intervention evidence exists.

graph_control_vs_centrality.centrality: degree/eigenvector/betweenness quantify different structural prominence properties
graph_control_vs_centrality.dominator: d dominates target v from root s iff every directed path s->v contains d
graph_control_vs_centrality.min_cut: a minimum cut identifies a smallest-capacity or smallest-cardinality bottleneck set under the chosen graph model
graph_control_vs_centrality.project_law: A hub can be bypassable; a low-degree dominator can be mandatory. Centrality and gatekeeping are therefore different.
graph_control_vs_centrality.door_relation: Door is strongest as mandatory gateway only when dominator/cut/reachability analysis supports that role in the declared graph.

agency_metrics.reachable_volume: mu(R(T,x0)) under a declared measure mu
agency_metrics.control_cost: minimum or expected intervention cost to reach a target set
agency_metrics.robust_reachability: states reachable despite an allowed disturbance set
agency_metrics.interpretation: Agency has multiple coordinates: number/volume of alternatives, robustness, cost, reversibility and ability to choose among them.

leash_owner_matrix.decision_rule: Only promote 'controller' when an intervention channel and outcome effect are evidenced; only promote 'owner' when ownership semantics are separately established.
leash_owner_matrix.project_use: Allows future maps to show center, observer, anchor, controller and owner as separate node-edge roles instead of one overloaded crown.

new_project_laws: Anchor Is Not Owner Law: geometric reference does not establish ownership.
Attention Is Not Control Law: being watched, orbited or central in discourse does not establish causal actuation.
Observation Is Not Actuation Law: Eye/measurement and Leash/control require different channels.
Centrality Is Not Dominance Law: high graph centrality need not make a node mandatory on source-target paths.
Control Requires Channel Law: causal control needs an intervention channel that changes state/reachability under a declared model.
Many-Controller Law: competing constraints and controllers can shape trajectories without any single actor owning the timeline.
Agency Is Reachability Plus Cost Law: having a reachable target is weaker than being able to reach it robustly and affordably.
Release Authority Law: a meaningful leash model should name who or what can relax, lengthen, move or remove the constraint.
